screens:
The session begins.

The Gilded Gull bumps against the pilings, and the gangplank thuds down onto wet planks. Baldur's Gate hits you all at once: tar, fish, smoke from a hundred chimneys, gulls screaming over the masts, and a dozen languages shouting over one another along the waterfront. Lamplighters are working their way down the quay as the sun sinks behind the harbour. Above the warehouse roofs, the city climbs in tiers towards the dark line of the inner wall.

At the foot of the gangplank, a Flaming Fist sergeant with a ledger and ink-stained fingers waves passengers forward one at a time. "Name, business, how long you're staying. Keep it moving." A lanky young porter is already trotting alongside the line, offering to carry bags to "the best beds in the Lower City, honest prices."

Your cat pauses on the rail and stares past them both. Beside a stack of crates stands a woman in a plain grey coat. She looks up at each face coming off the ship, then down at a folded paper in her hand, then up again. The passenger ahead of you gives his name to the sergeant. The ledger turns your way, and the woman's eyes lift towards the gangplank.

The Gate is in front of you, with the goddess's errand still unexplained. What do you do?

Your records:
James Worgen — Warlock 5th level, patron Tymora (Celestial), Pact of the Chain, level 5
HP 38/38 · AC 15 · Speed 30 feet
STR 9 · DEX 15 · CON 14 · INT 11 · WIS 13 · CHA 18
Skills: Deception +7 (Beguiling Influence); Persuasion +7 (Beguiling Influence); Intimidation +7 (soldier); Athletics +2 (soldier); Arcana +3 (warlock); Religion +3 (warlock); Stealth +2 (advantage on sound-based checks from Boots of Elvenkind); Perception +1 (passive Perception 11); Insight +1; Tool proficiency: playing cards; vehicles (land)
Saves: Strength saving throw +0 (Cloak of Protection +1); Dexterity saving throw +3 (Cloak of Protection +1); Constitution saving throw +3 (Cloak of Protection +1); Intelligence saving throw +1 (Cloak of Protection +1); Wisdom saving throw +5 (proficient, Cloak of Protection +1); Charisma saving throw +8 (proficient, Cloak of Protection +1)
Attacks: Eldritch Blast: +8 to hit, 2 beams, each 1d10+4 force, range 120 feet; Sacred Flame: DC 16 Dexterity save, 2d8 radiant, range 60 feet, ignores cover; Rapier: +5 to hit, 1d8+2 piercing, finesse; Light crossbow: +5 to hit, 1d8+2 piercing, range 80/320 feet, loading, two-handed; Spell attack +8, spell save DC 16 (with the Rod of the Pact Keeper)
Abilities: Proficiency bonus +3; Pact Magic: 2 pact slots, both 3rd level, recovered on a short or long rest. Spellcasting ability Charisma.; Patron, Tymora: the Lady of Luck grants celestial gifts. Light and Sacred Flame are bonus cantrips.; Healing Light: a pool of 6d6 per long rest. As a bonus action, heal a creature within 60 feet, spending up to 4 dice at a time.; Agonizing Blast: add +4 (CHA) to the damage of each Eldritch Blast beam.; Mask of Many Faces: cast Disguise Self at will, without a spell slot.; Beguiling Influence: proficiency in Deception and Persuasion.; Pact of the Chain: a cat familiar. Telepathy within 100 feet. He can use its senses, and it can deliver his touch spells.; Pact of the Chain: he can forgo one of his attacks so the familiar attacks with its reaction.; Familiar (cat): AC 12, HP 2, speed 40 ft, climb 30 ft. Perception +3, Stealth +4. Claws 1 slashing. Keen smell.; Military Rank (soldier): Tethyrian veterans and soldiers recognise his former rank and may lend aid or shelter.; Tymora's Envoy: he owes the goddess and is bound by her ban on cards. Her temples may recognise her mark on him.
Spells: Eldritch Blast (cantrip); Friends (cantrip); Prestidigitation (cantrip); Light (cantrip); Sacred Flame (cantrip); Hex (1); Guiding Bolt (1); Misty Step (2); Invisibility (2); Suggestion (2); Hypnotic Pattern (3); Disguise Self (Mask of Many Faces) (1); Find Familiar (Pact of the Chain) (1)
Limits: Light armour only; fragile in melee.; Only two pact slots: he must husband them between short rests.; Only one concentration spell at a time (Hex, Suggestion, Hypnotic Pattern, Invisibility, Friends).; Tymora's ban: he must not play cards. The temptation is strong, and others can use it against him.; The Rod of the Pact Keeper and the Cloak of Protection require attunement (2 of 3 slots used).
Counters: Hit dice 5/5; Healing light 6/6; Spell slots 3 2/2; Pact keeper rod 1/1
Money: 350 gp
Worn: Cloak: Tethyrian soldier's cloak (Cloak of Protection); Armor / clothing: Studded leather armour; Boots: Boots of Elvenkind; Main hand: Rapier
Pack: Coin of Tymora; Component pouch; Crossbow bolts ×20; Deck of cards; Explorer's pack; James's papers; Light crossbow; Potion of healing ×2; Rod of the Pact Keeper +1
Place: Lower City quay, Baldur's Gate
Time: Day 1 · evening

The sergeant doesn't look up until the name is half out, and then only long enough to check the face against it. His quill scratches across the page.

"Worgen. Sellsword." He blots the line with the side of his hand and adds to the smear already there. "Between companies, he says. Half the Lower City's between companies." He nods towards the harbour, where a squat tower stands black against the last of the sunset. "The Fist takes on men at the Seatower, if your tenday runs longer than your purse. Keep your blade sheathed on the docks and we'll get on fine. Next."

That's it. Nobody asks about the rapier or the cloak, and nobody so much as glances at the cat. James is in Baldur's Gate.

The porter falls in beside him before he's gone three steps. He's all elbows and knees, with a rope sling over one shoulder and a grin that's lost a tooth. "Carry your pack, sir? The Three Old Kegs, the Elfsong if you've got coin for it, or a place I know that's cheaper than both and the fleas are mostly polite." Then he sees where James is looking and drops his voice, sounding more curious than anything. "Her? Been on this quay every evening this tenday. Meets every ship from the south, never says a word to anyone, goes home when the last one's empty. Thought she was waiting on a husband."

The cat pads silently down beside James's boots. Through the link comes a smell the harbour doesn't have: beeswax, and under it something sweet and burnt, the way a chapel smells after the candles are out. It's coming off the paper in the woman's hand.

She has stopped looking at the other faces. Her eyes go from the cat to the worn regimental cloak, down to the paper one last time, and then she folds it shut and steps away from the crates. Up close she's younger than her coat. She has ink on her thumb, like the sergeant, and she looks like she hasn't slept much.

"Forgive me. I heard you give your name." She keeps her voice under the noise of the quay, and it's steadier than her hands. "I was sent to meet a man off a southern ship at sundown, a soldier's cloak and a cat walking ahead of him. Those were the words I was given. Nothing more, I'm afraid. No name." She takes a short breath. "I'm Ysolde Crane. Will you walk with me a little way, Master Worgen? It isn't far, and I'd rather not say the rest in front of the Fist."

Pell Marrow pretends very hard to be looking at the gulls.

· Time passes: 5 minutes
· The cat joins you
· New place: Seatower of Balduran
· Main arc: Envoy of Luck

Party: The cat (HP 2/2)
Goal: Envoy of Luck
The arc: Envoy of Luck

Place: Lower City quay, Baldur's Gate · Time: Day 1 · evening

Pell Marrow takes being ignored like a man who's had worse. "Suit yourself, sir. Kegs is up Brindle Lane if the lady's errand runs short." He's already turning back to the gangplank, where a merchant with three trunks has started shouting for help.

Ysolde doesn't answer straight away. She leads him off the quay between two warehouses into a lane that smells of wet rope, where the noise of the harbour drops to a murmur behind them. She looks back once. The sergeant's lamp is a smudge of orange at the bottom of the slope, and nobody is following them. Only then does she unfold the paper and hold it out where the light from a chandler's window falls on it.

"It's the whole of it," she says. "I didn't write it. I've only carried it."

It's good paper, heavier than a clerk would waste, with one round drop of pale wax dried at the corner. The writing is an older hand, steady and upright, set out in short lines:

*A southern ship at sundown.
A soldier's cloak. A cat before him.
Bring him to the Lady before the gate shuts.*

Under that, smaller and pressed harder, as if the pen had stopped and then gone on:

*Do not ask him to swear.*

The smell comes off it again, close up this time: beeswax and snuffed candles. James has stood in enough of the goddess's shrines along the southern coast to know that incense. Tymora's priests burn it at the evening toss.

"The High Priestess of the Lady's Hall wrote that," Ysolde says. She takes the paper back and folds it along the old creases. "I'm a scribe there. I copy contracts and dedications. I don't go out on errands as a rule, and I've never been sent to meet a stranger off a boat before." She hesitates. "I don't know what the last line means. I asked her, and she said I would understand it once you had or hadn't. That was all I got."

She rubs at the ink on her thumb, then seems to notice and stops.

"The Hall is in the Upper City. The Watch shuts the inner gates a little after full dark, and anyone without business gets turned back until morning. I have a pass that will take one guest through tonight." She looks up the lane to where it climbs between the rooftops towards the black line of the wall. "If we go now there's time, but not much. Forgive me for asking it of a man an hour off a ship, Master Worgen. Will you come?"

---

Place: Rope lane above the quay · Time: Day 1 · evening

Ysolde starts uphill before he's finished, the way people do when they've been watching the light go all evening. The lane narrows and turns into steps, worn hollow in the middle, between a cooper's yard and a row of shuttered counting-rooms. Above the roofs the sky has gone from orange to the colour of a bruise.

"The High Priestess, of course," she says, a little short of breath on the climb. "Brother Tamsin keeps the door at the Hall. He writes out the pass for me every evening and burns the old one, so he knows. The Watch at the Basilisk Gate have watched me go down ten nights running. They stopped asking on the third." She stops to think about it on the next landing, then goes on climbing. "And anyone who works the quay, I suppose. I didn't think of it as hiding. I wear this coat so I won't be noticed, not so I can't be."

James keeps his pace and lets his eyes go to the glass. There's a glazier's window, a pawnbroker's, then the dark pane of a chandlery that's shut for the night.

messages.text:
James steps down off the gangplank, letting the cat drop silently to the planks beside him. He gives the sergeant an easy, tired nod.

"James Worgen. Sellsword between companies. Here for work and a bed — a tenday, maybe longer, if the Gate has use for me."

As he says it, he lets his eyes drift once toward the woman in grey, and he's aware of the cat already watching her from the rail.

James glances once after the sergeant, then down at the cat, then back to her face. The cat's stillness tells him what the quay doesn't: someone in a grey coat has been reading a paper that smells like candles gone out.

"Ysolde Crane." He says the name as if testing it. "You haven't asked the porter to carry your message, so it either isn't for him or it costs more than six coppers. Walk where you like. I'll keep a step off your heel."

He hoists the strap of his pack higher and lets the female porter's grin go unacknowledged. The cat trots ahead of him, not far, ears angled back just enough to listen. James falls in beside her as they go, eyes moving along the quay.

"Only one thing before you tell me the rest," he says, low. "The paper in your hand — is that one of the words, or the whole message?"

James hasn't looked away from the folded paper since she put it away. The smell of it stays at the back of his throat, the cool end of incense after a long evening in a shrine tent. Tymora's hall. In the Upper City, behind a wall that shuts like a portcullis on whoever's outside it.

He glances up the lane towards the wall, then back at her.

"A temple scribe with a pass for one guest, and a message that says not to ask me for an oath. That last line wasn't written for you." He keeps it low, just between them. "Were I a different sort of man, I'd ask how the High Priestess knew which ship and which cloak. But I've learned not to waste questions on a goddess's aim." A pause, half a smile, gone fast. "I'm her man for now. Let's not be late."

He shifts the pack once, settles it, and gestures with two fingers. Not a wave so much as permission. The cat, which has been sitting in the shadow of a drainpipe at the mouth of the lane, rises and paces ahead of Ysolde, tail high.

"One thing before the wall," James says as they start up. "Does anyone else know the Lady's people sent you to the quay? A watchman's son, a nosy deacon, a porter with a better memory than Pell?"

He walks a pace behind and a little to her right, where he can watch both her face and the lane behind them in shopfront glass.

The cat's gone ahead a little, light-footed on the wet stone.

[🎲] The die settles: an 8, and with the +2 for his eye and the glass, James makes a 10.

He studies the windows as they climb — a glazier's, a pawnbroker's, then the chandler's dark pane — but the lamplight behind them is poor, and the lane keeps bending. No one matches their pace, nobody lingers at the turnings; only two men rolling a barrel up from the cooper's yard, who don't look up. If there's a tail, it's better than his view of it.

The cat has gone ahead, a pale shape pausing at the top of the steps. Through the link, the city's smell sharpens: a gate-fire burning pine cones, old mud, something fish-rotten from the drains.

Ysolde takes the last steps with a hand on the rail and points. "The Basilisk Gate. We're in time."

The inner wall rises over them, black basalt patched with grey, and before it a gatehouse with a brazier on either side. The Watch are closing up — one is turning the handles of a great iron lamp, another calls to a porter to move his cart off the stone because the gate will not wait for wineskins. The men at the doors wear the red-and-gold of the Watch, not the Fist's black, and they check passes with a small careless lamp.

Ysolde straightens her coat, takes out the folded paper from inside it, and walks you towards them.

The scene waits for James now.

Ysolde is already walking up to the Watch, the folded paper in her hand. The gatehouse looms behind the braziers; the Watch are checking passes and glancing at the sky, and the two men at the doors have looked your way once and gone back to standing their watch. If you mean to present yourself as her guest, this is the moment — say a word to her, straighten your cloak, flash that easy soldier's nod. Otherwise the gate will not wait.

What do you do?

A note from the player:

What worked: The opening pulled me right in — the harbour, the smells, the sergeant's tired routine, and Ysolde stepping out from the crates all felt like a real evening in the Gate. The mystery is set up well: the paper with the wax and the incense, the line "Do not ask him to swear," the fact that the High Priestess knew my ship and my cloak. That's exactly the kind of hook that makes me want to know what Tymora's errand is. Ysolde herself is a good NPC: tired, careful, quietly scared, and not stupid. I liked that she quoted the message rather than handing me the paper to keep. The cat's observation through the link (beeswax, snuffed candles) was a nice touch, and it reminded me of the familiar's usefulness without being intrusive.

The roll card and the server die worked cleanly. I knew what I was rolling for, what the bonus was, and the result was narrated without breaking the scene. The failed Perception check felt fair — the lane was dark and the shop windows weren't much help. I also appreciated the out-of-game clarification about Pell Marrow's gender; that kind of care keeps the table smooth.

What broke or felt missing: Nothing broke, but a couple of things could have been tighter. The turn before the roll card felt slightly delayed — I typed a message, but then the card appeared, and I had to wait again. In a text-based game that's fine, but a tiny note like "Rolling now — tap the die when ready" might have removed the feeling of a dead stop. Also, the session ended right at the Watch. I would have liked a little more time to choose how James presents himself — a chance to use Deception or Persuasion, or to read the Watch's mood before Ysolde takes over. That said, as a cliffhanger it's strong; I just hope the next session starts with my choice, not with the gate already swinging open.

What's missing so far: Not much. The crew-gathering aspect of the "Ocean's Eleven" wish hasn't come up yet, but it's early. I'd like to see more of the city's underside eventually — the porter mentioned the Three Old Kegs, and the Undercellar is already in my head. A small thing: the "do not ask him to swear" line made me think we might need to establish whether James has any actual oath to Tymora or just a debt; if there's a mechanical or narrative difference, I hope that becomes clear soon. Overall, this is a promising start, and I'm curious what's behind the wall.

Yes — the moment at the Basilisk Gate. I wanted James to pause just before Ysolde reached the Watch, to take in the two men at the doors and read whether they were bored, on edge, or looking for a bribe. More than that, I wanted a chance to decide *how* to present himself — give them the easy sellsword nod, let them see the Tethyrian cloak and assume I'm just a hired blade with a temple scribe, or quietly step forward and do the talking myself with Deception or Persuasion. The session ended on that threshold before I could act, so it felt like the choice was about to be made *for* me. That's the only time I had a clear "I wish I'd done that" feeling — not out of frustration, just from the cliffhanger landing right as I was reaching for the next move.

The cat has gone ahead, a pale shape pausing at the top of the steps. Through the link, the city's smell sharpens: a gate-fire burning pine cones, old mud, something fish-rotten from the drains.

Ysolde takes the last steps with a hand on the rail and points. "The Basilisk Gate. We're in time."

The inner wall rises over them, black basalt patched with grey, and before it a gatehouse with a brazier on either side. The Watch are closing up — one is turning the handles of a great iron lamp, another calls to a porter to move his cart off the stone because the gate will not wait for wineskins. The men at the doors wear the red-and-gold of the Watch, not the Fist's black, and they check passes with a small careless lamp.

Ysolde straightens her coat, takes out the folded paper from inside it, and walks you towards them.

The scene waits for James now.

Ysolde is already walking up to the Watch, the folded paper in her hand. The gatehouse looms behind the braziers; the Watch are checking passes and glancing at the sky, and the two men at the doors have looked your way once and gone back to standing their watch. If you mean to present yourself as her guest, this is the moment — say a word to her, straighten your cloak, flash that easy soldier's nod. Otherwise the gate will not wait.

What do you do?

note.text:
A note from the player:

What worked: The opening pulled me right in — the harbour, the smells, the sergeant's tired routine, and Ysolde stepping out from the crates all felt like a real evening in the Gate. The mystery is set up well: the paper with the wax and the incense, the line "Do not ask him to swear," the fact that the High Priestess knew my ship and my cloak. That's exactly the kind of hook that makes me want to know what Tymora's errand is. Ysolde herself is a good NPC: tired, careful, quietly scared, and not stupid. I liked that she quoted the message rather than handing me the paper to keep. The cat's observation through the link (beeswax, snuffed candles) was a nice touch, and it reminded me of the familiar's usefulness without being intrusive.

The roll card and the server die worked cleanly. I knew what I was rolling for, what the bonus was, and the result was narrated without breaking the scene. The failed Perception check felt fair — the lane was dark and the shop windows weren't much help. I also appreciated the out-of-game clarification about Pell Marrow's gender; that kind of care keeps the table smooth.

What broke or felt missing: Nothing broke, but a couple of things could have been tighter. The turn before the roll card felt slightly delayed — I typed a message, but then the card appeared, and I had to wait again. In a text-based game that's fine, but a tiny note like "Rolling now — tap the die when ready" might have removed the feeling of a dead stop. Also, the session ended right at the Watch. I would have liked a little more time to choose how James presents himself — a chance to use Deception or Persuasion, or to read the Watch's mood before Ysolde takes over. That said, as a cliffhanger it's strong; I just hope the next session starts with my choice, not with the gate already swinging open.

What's missing so far: Not much. The crew-gathering aspect of the "Ocean's Eleven" wish hasn't come up yet, but it's early. I'd like to see more of the city's underside eventually — the porter mentioned the Three Old Kegs, and the Undercellar is already in my head. A small thing: the "do not ask him to swear" line made me think we might need to establish whether James has any actual oath to Tymora or just a debt; if there's a mechanical or narrative difference, I hope that becomes clear soon. Overall, this is a promising start, and I'm curious what's behind the wall.

after.text: Yes — the moment at the Basilisk Gate. I wanted James to pause just before Ysolde reached the Watch, to take in the two men at the doors and read whether they were bored, on edge, or looking for a bribe. More than that, I wanted a chance to decide *how* to present himself — give them the easy sellsword nod, let them see the Tethyrian cloak and assume I'm just a hired blade with a temple scribe, or quietly step forward and do the talking myself with Deception or Persuasion. The session ended on that threshold before I could act, so it felt like the choice was about to be made *for* me. That's the only time I had a clear "I wish I'd done that" feeling — not out of frustration, just from the cliffhanger landing right as I was reaching for the next move.

opening.text:
The Gilded Gull bumps against the pilings, and the gangplank thuds down onto wet planks. Baldur's Gate hits you all at once: tar, fish, smoke from a hundred chimneys, gulls screaming over the masts, and a dozen languages shouting over one another along the waterfront. Lamplighters are working their way down the quay as the sun sinks behind the harbour. Above the warehouse roofs, the city climbs in tiers towards the dark line of the inner wall.

At the foot of the gangplank, a Flaming Fist sergeant with a ledger and ink-stained fingers waves passengers forward one at a time. "Name, business, how long you're staying. Keep it moving." A lanky young porter is already trotting alongside the line, offering to carry bags to "the best beds in the Lower City, honest prices."

Your cat pauses on the rail and stares past them both. Beside a stack of crates stands a woman in a plain grey coat. She looks up at each face coming off the ship, then down at a folded paper in her hand, then up again. The passenger ahead of you gives his name to the sergeant. The ledger turns your way, and the woman's eyes lift towards the gangplank.

The Gate is in front of you, with the goddess's errand still unexplained. What do you do?
